newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht slump weighs on regionals.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht slump weighs on regionals.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies remained prone to wild swings on Wednesday as liquidity dwindled and players turned increasingly cautious ahead of an Asian central bankers meeting.

Expectations the Friday meeting in Shanghai might result in some form of coordinated intervention to counter the recent speculative onslaught on the region's currencies kept the dollar well bid against the regionals.

"The big issue for the market at the moment is this meeting in Shanghai as there is the possibility of concerted intervention or a statement that they are willing to join hands to support currencies," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
The meeting is being hosted by the People's Bank of China and the participants were due to arrive in Shanghai on Thursday evening.
Those attending include Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, The Philippines, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, China and Indonesia.
In Thailand, the baht sank to new lows on heavy commercial demand for dollars.
The move towards the 32 baht level against the dollar put pressure on the baht in offshore markets as well, dealers said.

Bangkok dealers said most of the buying was from corporates and importers. "I suspect corporates bought dollars to repay their foreign debt but I did not notice any panic buying," a foreign bank dealer said.
"The market was fairly thin actually, and there were virtually no buyers of the baht. So any small dollar buying can exaggerate the market," he said.
Others said jitters over soon-to-be-released non-performing loans data of financial institutions could also have spurred the dollar buying.

"There has been this market talk about some foreign financial institutions having stopped rolling over their loans to Thai corporates. I don't know if that is related to the high demand for dollars now," said another dealer.
Singapore dealers said the baht showed potential to weaken as far as 35 against the U.S. dollar eventually.
The Thai unit was quoted at 31.800/32.100 to the dollar onshore at 0425 GMT. It was at 30.700/31.200 offshore.
The baht's weakness knocked the wind out of the Indonesian rupiah, which had earlier shown signs of recovering towards the 2,500 level, dealers said.
A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said the pressure on the baht immediately spilled over to the rupiah, sending the rupiah down to 2,570 from a high of 2,535.0.
It was quoted at 2,570/600 at 0425 GMT against an opening 2,570/80.
The Malaysian ringgit remained weak, trading in a wide band as spreads remained wide and volumes thin, dealers said.
"There's a 30-point spread being quoted. Liquidity is very bad. Even the big Americans are only trading in one or two (million) dollars," a Singapore dealer said.
She said the market was still expecting Malaysia to impose some form of capital controls following Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's return from a two-month overseas trip on Tuesday.
Mahathir declined to comment on the ringgit but said he was uncomfortable with the power wielded by speculators.
Rumours that Southeast Asian central banks were checking the books of all banks to trace the source of recent regional currency instability earlier lent brief strength to the regional currencies.
The Singapore dollar came under renewed pressure, slipping back beyond the 1.46 level to the U.S. dollar.
Dealers said dollar/Sing was looking slightly overbought and tightness in domestic interest rates would cushion the Singapore dollar's downside.
"I expect a retracement to the 1.4550 level, where I would buy back the U.S. dollar to see it above 1.48," a dealer said.
The Philippine peso weakened to 28.400/520 at 0425 GMT against its close at 28.15 on Tuesday.
The central bank's new ruling aimed at encouraging banks to sell dollars and curb speculation had little immediate impact as banks bought dollars to meet import demand, Manila traders said.

The Philippine central bank cut the overbought dollar limit of banks to 10 percent from 20 percent of their unimpaired capital. It also raised the oversold dollar limit of banks to 20 percent from 10 percent previously.
